title: Designing a chat service like WhatsApp

facts.text: Support one-on-one chat, group chats of at most 100 people and file sharing, with high availability and minimal latency; extended requirements are sent, delivered and read receipts, last seen time and push notifications.

Assume 50 million daily active users each sending at least 10 messages to 4 different people a day: 2 billion messages per day, or 24K requests per second, with 5 percent of messages being media files.
At 100 bytes per message, text needs about 200 GB a day and 100 KB media files need 10 TB a day, about 38 PB over 10 years; 10.2 TB of daily ingress needs around 120 MB per second.

Tables are users (name, phoneNumber), messages (type, content, timestamps, chatID or groupID), chats, groups and the N:M tables users_chats and users_groups; services each own a table, in PostgreSQL or a distributed NoSQL store like Cassandra.
The API offers Get all chats or groups for a user ID, Get messages for a user ID and channel ID, Send message (user ID, channel ID, message) returning a boolean result, and Join or leave a channel.

Microservices scale horizontally and decouple, each owning its data: a user service (HTTP, authentication), chat service, notification service, presence service for last seen and media service for uploads, talking over REST or lighter gRPC.

Pulling by periodic HTTP requests or long polling is not scalable, since most responses are empty; push over WebSockets delivers data without delay and is full-duplex, unlike one-way Server-Sent Events, and a cache of active connections shows who is online.

The sender's chat service has the sequencing service give the message a unique ID, persists it and queues it for sync; if the recipient is online it is pushed over their web socket, otherwise via the push server.

On login the client opens a web socket and the presence service updates the user's status and notifies friends; last seen uses a client heartbeat ping, with the last active timestamp kept in a Redis or Memcached cache.

If the recipient is not active, the chat service queues an event with device-platform metadata; the notification service forwards it to Firebase Cloud Messaging or Apple Push Notification Service, and queues give best-effort ordering and at-least-once delivery.
A client acknowledgment (ACK) shows a message was delivered and sets its deliveredAt field, and the message is marked seen, setting seenAt, once the user opens the chat.

Partition the database horizontally by hash, list, range or composite schemes, with consistent hashing against uneven load; cache older messages with LRU eviction and paginate group history so limited-bandwidth users load old messages only on request.

Most storage is media, handled by the media service in object storage such as Amazon S3, Azure Blob Storage or Google Cloud Storage, or HDFS or GlusterFS, with static files served from a CDN such as CloudFront or Cloudflare.

Remove single points of failure with multiple service instances, load balancers, read replicas, a replicated cache and a standby API Gateway, the one entry point for HTTP, WebSocket and TCP/IP; use Kafka or NATS for robust notifications.

WhatsApp itself uses store and forward: its server stores a message, tries to forward it to the addressee and repeatedly requests acknowledgement of receipt, deleting it once acknowledged or, if undelivered, after 30 days.
Multimedia is sent by uploading the image, audio or video to an HTTP server, then sending a link to the content with its Base64 encoded thumbnail where applicable.

notes: Singh's design continues in chunk 02 with two facts on real WhatsApp delivery (store and forward, media links). Left out for the 16-fact cap: API gateway features (authentication, rate limiting), the lazy last-seen alternative (30 seconds without action), media compression and a separate group service as detail.; Redraft of the chunk 01 Worked example: only the new facts.

definition.text: Instant messaging is synchronous communication that sends messages in real time between two or more parties over the Internet or another computer network.

facts.text: It covers private messaging between two users and chat rooms or groups, allowing immediate receipt of acknowledgment or reply, in contrast to email, where conversations are not real-time.
Modern messaging apps go beyond text to multimedia, emojis, file transfer, voice calling and video chat, and connect known users through a contact list or chat rooms.

Modern services provide their own client, either an installed application or a browser-based one, and run as centralised networks on the operator's servers, unlike peer-to-peer protocols such as XMPP.
Most instant messaging protocols are proprietary and not interoperable, so users cannot reach people on other networks.
Messages may be kept in local device storage or in cloud-based server storage; cloud storage carries an increased risk that the provider may hold the decryption keys and view saved messages.
Encryption is the primary way messaging apps protect users' privacy and security, and privacy can be enhanced with end-to-end encryption by default.

definition.text: A simple chat application can be built on Redis publish-subscribe, with the server publishing each chat message to a topic that subscribers pick up.

facts.text: A web socket connects client and server, and the pub-sub server opens several connections to Redis: one updates the data models and publishes to a topic, the others subscribe and listen for topic updates.
On connecting, the client gets the chat member list and the historical messages from Redis, and a new member is announced by publishing to the member_add topic so other participants can see them.
A new chat message is added to a Redis sorted set with zadd, sorted by arrival time, and the pub-sub server publishes it to the messages topic so the recipient's client receives it.

title: How WhatsApp delivers messages

definition.text: WhatsApp runs a customized version of the open XMPP protocol and delivers messages by store and forward.

facts.text: The protocol is a customized version of the open standard Extensible messaging and presence protocol (XMPP), named FunXMPP in a 2019 US Department of Justice document.
An account uses the phone number as username, and the app compares the address book's numbers with the central database of users to add contacts to the contact list automatically.

Store and forward: a message is stored on a server, which tries to forward it and repeatedly requests acknowledgement; once acknowledged it is deleted, and if undelivered after 30 days it is deleted too.
A multimedia message is uploaded to an HTTP server, and only a link to the content, plus a Base64 encoded thumbnail where applicable, is sent in the message.
Messages are encrypted with the Signal Protocol, end-to-end encryption was completed for every form of communication in April 2016, users can verify each other's keys, and calls use SRTP.
Linked devices, up to four per account, sync with the primary phone; the phone originally had to stay online for them to work, but multi-device support removed that requirement.
WhatsApp handled ten billion messages per day in August 2012, up from two billion in April 2012.

notes: Tech-stack and company-history sentences of the WhatsApp article are deliberately not used.
